analysis.title: Inverting Policy Is Warsh's Challenge
key_insights: Steven Blitz argues that raising the funds rate to invert the curve would be symbolic but ultimately ineffective. His preferred path is to hold the short end, let the long end rise, and allow risk preferences to reset.
Blitz still expects Warsh to find a way through the CPI data to avoid a September hike, which would let the curve steepen. He says Warsh and Bessent are already thinking about this approach.

Private sector credit is a shrinking share of total debt creation, so slowing the economy through higher short rates requires a much larger contraction in private credit. The private sector is less leveraged, its debt has longer maturity, and a large liquidity overhang remains.
The Federal government borrows regardless of interest rates and so supports growth and inflation. Since 2012, inflation has tracked Federal borrowing more closely than private borrowing.

Corporate immunity to higher short rates and the larger Federal share of borrowing mean an inverted 3M-10Y curve now takes longer to produce a recession. The last inversion lasted 25 months and did not flip the economy into recession.
Blitz suggests Bessent and Warsh may hold the funds rate so Treasury can borrow more cheaply at the short end, while the market sets 10-year yields to match supply and demand for funds.

In his view the bond market is not in trouble. Yields are still too low to slow nominal spending, and the Fed and Treasury can let them rise at a measured, managed pace, which is the purpose of the buybacks according to Bessent.

The Fed could speed up steepening by letting the repo-IORB spread widen. This would raise leverage costs and curtail asset-buying leverage without the credibility cost of a rate hike, especially given hedge funds now hold a larger share of Treasuries.

Household credit use has not recovered since the GFC. The ratio of credit card balances to retail sales ex-autos is below pre-GFC levels, and the small post-Covid bounce has reversed as card interest rates surged.

Household margin debt has risen in line with equity values and is still not back to pre-Covid levels relative to them. A higher funds rate would affect margin buying, but by less than the raw margin numbers suggest.
If the Fed does hike, the usual trade of buying 30-year and selling 10-year Treasuries may not work this time. Blitz would fade the initial market reaction in the 10Y forward versus spot spread.
The 10Y forward yield has narrowed to the spot yield since the start of the year, and historically that spread reverses when the Fed starts hiking. Blitz is not convinced it will this time.

Blitz says Trump's handling of foreign capital flows is a dangerous game for US capital markets, but there is no real alternative destination for capital at the size needed to absorb the roughly 3% of US GDP the US sends abroad to supply dollars.
CPI on Friday will be examined for a reason for Warsh not to hike. Blitz says Warsh's task force may convince the FOMC that a steeper curve is better than an inverted one.

macro_indicators.reading: Possible 25bp hike in September, which Blitz expects Warsh to avoid
macro_indicators.interpretation: Blitz expects Warsh to hold in September and says a 25bp hike would be symbolic. He sees a steeper curve as the better outcome.

macro_indicators.reading: Last inversion began Nov-22 and lasted 25 months without a recession
macro_indicators.interpretation: Inversion has become a less reliable recession signal because of lower corporate rate sensitivity and the larger Federal share of borrowing.

macro_indicators.indicator: Federal government share of nonfinancial borrowing
macro_indicators.interpretation: Federal borrowing is not sensitive to rates, which blunts the effect of monetary tightening.

macro_indicators.indicator: Nonfinancial corporate CP + bank loans as % of bonds
macro_indicators.interpretation: Corporate debt is mostly fixed-rate bonds, so short-rate hikes pass through less.

macro_indicators.reading: Release due Friday, no figure cited
macro_indicators.interpretation: The CPI data will be scrutinized for a reason for the Fed to hold rather than hike in September.

macro_indicators.indicator: US dollar outflow to the rest of the world
macro_indicators.interpretation: No alternative destination exists for capital at a size that could absorb this outflow, which supports US markets for now.

trade_ideas.description: Fade the initial market reaction in the 10Y forward versus spot yield spread if the Fed hikes
trade_ideas.rationale: Historically the spread reverses when the Fed starts to hike, but Blitz is not convinced it will this time.

risk_factors: A Fed hike would be symbolic but could still disrupt markets and fail to slow inflation.
Foreign capital could be redirected away from the US because of Trump's actions.
Inflation remains driven by Federal borrowing, which does not respond to interest rates.
The market could be wrong on how high the funds rate must go to slow the economy.
charts_described: Table 1 shows that at the Nov-22 inversion nonfinancial corporate CP plus bank loans were 21% of bonds and Federal borrowing was 38% of nonfinancial borrowing, versus 55% to 74% and 19% to 24% in earlier inversions.
Chart 6 plots the 10Y forward minus spot yield spread against the Fed funds rate, and the text says the spread has historically reversed when the Fed hikes.
vol_and_positioning: Household margin debt has risen in line with equity values and remains below pre-Covid levels relative to them.
Hedge funds hold a higher share of outstanding Treasuries, which makes repo-rate leverage costs more relevant to asset buying.
The 10Y yield 10Y forward has narrowed to the spot yield this year. Historically the spread reverses when the Fed hikes.
geopolitical: Blitz says Trump is playing a dangerous game with how much the rest of the world redirects capital away from the US.

tension_points.bull_case: A steeper curve, with the funds rate held and long yields rising, slows inflation better than an inversion. Treasury borrows cheaply at the short end and the market sets long yields.
tension_points.bear_case: A hold in September may leave inflation unchecked if CPI is hot. A hike would be symbolic and could trigger an initial rise in forward yields.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A CPI print on Friday that leaves Warsh unable to avoid a September hike.

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher short rates are less effective because private borrowing is a smaller share of debt creation and Federal borrowing ignores rates.
theme_stances.evidence: Raise the funds rate & invert the curve! Symbolic but ultimately ineffective.

theme_stances.key_argument: Warsh likely finds a way through the CPI data to avoid a September hike and let the curve steepen.
theme_stances.evidence: Warsh finds a way through the CPI data to avert a Sep hike
